video.title: He Makes $4,100/Month Inspecting Houses (No Experience Needed)

summary: Lou describes doing residential construction draw inspections for lenders: visiting building sites, taking location-verified photos, and reporting whether work on the lender’s checklist is complete. He gets most of this work through inspection platforms, prices per visit, and schedules routes around a large rural service area. He also describes monthly condition checks for short-term rentals and a planned training business for new draw inspectors. The work has low overhead, but site visits and travel remain physical and the amount of work depends on local construction activity.

speakers.name: Nick
speakers.description: Host of the Side Hustle Show; the transcript gives his first name.

speakers.name: Lou
speakers.description: Draw inspector and former military and government inspector; the transcript’s rendering of his surname is unclear.

ideas.name: Residential construction draw inspections
ideas.one_liner: Visit a home under construction, document completed work with photos, and report to a lender so it can assess a construction-loan draw.
ideas.business_model: Per inspection, paid through lender-facing inspection companies and platforms.
ideas.customer: Banks, lenders, and inspection companies arranging construction-loan draw checks; builders or homeowners may be the site contact.
ideas.problem: Lenders cannot directly observe each construction site and want to verify reported progress before releasing loan funds.
ideas.offer: Visit the site, confirm the location, follow the lender’s inspection sheet, photograph work that is present and relevant work that is not yet present, and submit a report.

pricing.model: Per inspection; the inspector sets a price on some platforms, while other requests are offered at a stated fee.

price_points.label: A platform request price that Lou saw
Example of the request price rising after no takers

pricing.notes: Lou says prices vary by platform and location. He priced competitively to get work. The $45 and $55 figures are examples of a platform offer, not a stated standard rate.

acquisition_channels.details: Lou signed up with Nationwide Loan Inspectors and received requests by email. He also gets work through Built, Raise (rendered as R-A-Z-E in the transcript), and other inspection services. Built provides an app and lender-facing inspector selection; another platform emails jobs for inspectors to accept or bid on.

quote.text: I signed up with a company called Nationwide Loan Inspectors. Great folks, we're the majority of my business in 2025.
quote.speaker: Lou

acquisition_channels.details: A friend connected Lou to the work, and an experienced inspector mentored him. Lou says his mentor has built relationships with banks. Lou considered visiting local banks but chose not to pursue direct outreach because he wanted to keep the work part time.

ideas.delivery: The inspector accepts a request, contacts the builder or homeowner to arrange access, travels to the site, follows the lender's checklist, takes photos, and uploads a report. Lou says most site visits take about 25–30 minutes, but he spends substantial time driving. Some platforms accept reports in an app; others require uploading photos and completing forms on a website. Lou does this work himself and sometimes takes his wife along.
unit_economics_claims: Lou says he typically charges $60–$75 and averages about $65 per inspection.
Lou says monthly income averaged about $4,100 and lists about $972 in monthly expenses, including gas, software, insurance, phone, and internet.
Lou says he worked about 91 hours a month and usually worked two or three days a week.
Lou reports travel of roughly 200–250 miles on some workdays, so drive time materially affects the hourly return.
tools: Nationwide Loan Inspectors email and website
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. Lou describes low overhead and later reports operating expenses of about $972 per month; that is not a startup-cost figure.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated for Lou. He says his daughter earned about $1,200–$1,500 over six weeks after he mentored her, including two weeks when she was on vacation.

acquisition.how: Platforms route inspection requests and allow inspectors to accept or bid, but the inspector must sign up, price work, build relationships, and decide which jobs to take. Platform-based inbound requests can be handled in software.

onboarding.how: Requests arrive through apps or email, but the inspector reviews them, accepts them, contacts the site contact, and schedules access.

delivery.how: The inspector must physically travel to each construction site, inspect the checklist items, take photos, and document the site.

billing.how: Lou says he does not invoice; the platforms or inspection companies pay automatically on differing schedules. Payment tracking may still require human review.

support.how: Routine request and submission details may be handled in platform tools, but the inspector must resolve access, site, and report questions.

uk_applicability.notes: The underlying lender need and photo-based site checks could apply in the UK, but the transcript describes US lenders, platforms, loan practices, and business structures. UK lender requirements, construction-loan processes, insurance, and platform access would need checking.

risks: Work volume depends on construction activity in the inspector's service area and may be cyclical.
Travel can consume more time and money than the site visit; remote or low-construction areas may not support enough jobs.
Reports are expected quickly: Lou says inspection companies usually want them back within 24–48 hours.
A site visit creates physical safety and property-damage risks, including fresh concrete, finished floors, unsecured doors, and elevated decks without handrails.
Stay within the bank's checklist and document what is present; do not give construction-quality opinions or credit for items that are not installed.
Competitive pricing may be needed to win platform requests, and the transcript gives no guaranteed volume or standard rate.
Location and photo verification matter: Lou uses parcel records and geotagged photos to show that he visited the correct property.

ideas.name: Short-term rental condition and maintenance checks
ideas.one_liner: Visit a short-term rental periodically, check its condition and routine maintenance, and send the owner a photo report.
ideas.business_model: Per-visit fee; the host also suggests a possible monthly subscription, but Lou does not say he charges that subscription price.
ideas.customer: Short-term rental owners who live far away and local property managers.
ideas.problem: Owners who are not nearby want eyes and ears on their property, including checks between guests or alongside cleaner visits.
ideas.offer: Check filters, doors, windows, damage, and general condition; take photos and report issues. Lou also describes doing minor preparation such as changing a filter or dusting, and offering to connect owners with people who can handle larger work.

pricing.model: Per inspection visit; a monthly subscription was suggested by the host but not reported as an actual sale.
pricing.notes: Lou says he spends about an hour to an hour and a half on a check. He says he underpriced an initial large seven-bedroom property, but does not state its price.

acquisition_channels.details: Lou posted in a couple of Facebook pages asking whether anyone needed an inspector.

quote.text: I went to a couple of Facebook pages and said, "Hey, does anybody need an inspector?"
quote.speaker: Lou

acquisition_channels.details: Lou contacted a local project manager at a real-estate company who managed short-term rentals; one owner took him up on the service.

quote.text: I also reached out to a local project manager with a real estate company and said, "You know, she managed all their short-term rentals."
quote.speaker: Lou

ideas.delivery: Lou visits the property, follows a Tap Inspect checklist, takes photos, and submits a report on the home's condition. He checks items such as filters, locks, damage, and whether the grass has been cut. He sometimes does small tasks such as changing a filter or dusting, and offers to help find someone for larger repairs.
unit_economics_claims: Lou says he charges about $150 per visit and usually spends an hour and a half there.
The host proposes $200 per month as a hypothetical price for routine checks; Lou does not say he uses that price.
Lou says a large initial property took longer than he expected and he underpriced it.

acquisition.how: Posting in relevant groups and referrals through a property manager can generate leads, but service-area relationships and owner trust remain human-led. Any direct electronic marketing to individuals in the UK would need to comply with PECR and platform rules.

onboarding.how: A checklist and reporting app can standardize intake, but an owner must agree access, timing, and the scope of checks.

delivery.how: A person must physically visit the property and inspect it; filter changes, dusting, and other routine tasks also require physical work.

billing.how: A per-visit or subscription charge could be billed by software, but Lou does not describe an automated billing setup.

support.how: The inspector must assess and communicate property issues and may need to help the owner find a local person to resolve them.

uk_applicability.notes: Remote owners and short-term rental properties exist in the UK, and the inspection tasks are broadly transferable. Local access arrangements, property standards, insurance, and rules for short-term lets would vary.

risks: A large property can take longer than expected; Lou says he underpriced a seven-bedroom initial job.
Entering a property means checking drawers and under beds for items guests have left; Lou specifically warns that this can include firearms and create liability.
Routine checks can uncover maintenance needs that require a separate qualified tradesperson.
The work is physical and local, so travel and access affect the economics.
The host's proposed monthly price is hypothetical and should not be treated as a proven rate.

ideas.name: Draw inspector training
ideas.one_liner: Teach prospective inspectors the fundamentals of construction draw inspections through training modules and mentoring.
ideas.business_model: Not stated; Lou is preparing a training website and modules, but gives no price or sales details.
ideas.customer: People who want to start doing construction draw inspections.
ideas.problem: Prospective inspectors may not know how to enter the field, what the work involves, or how to handle its platforms and self-employment basics.
ideas.offer: A planned website and eight training modules covering draw basics, banks, professional standards, ethics, construction fundamentals, platforms and apps, self-employment tips, and sole proprietor, S Corp, or LLC basics. Lou also says he wants to mentor other people.

pricing.notes: The training site is being prepared; the transcript gives no course or mentoring price.

ideas.delivery: Lou says the modules are nearly complete and that he wants to teach and mentor future inspectors. The delivery format, access model, and level of personal support are not stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated; the website is being prepared and modules are described as almost complete.

acquisition.how: No customer acquisition channel is stated. A course could be marketed online, but that is an estimate rather than a described process.

onboarding.how: A website and digital course could automate enrollment and access, but the transcript does not state how students will sign up.

delivery.how: Recorded modules could deliver much of the training repeatedly, but Lou also intends to mentor people, which requires human time.

billing.how: No payment system or billing process is stated.

support.how: Lou describes mentoring learners, which requires human involvement; no support automation is described.

uk_applicability.notes: The inspection concepts may transfer, but the planned modules explicitly include US business structures such as S Corp and LLC and are based on Lou's US platforms and lender practices. UK legal and tax content would need changes.

risks: The training business is planned, not demonstrated; there are no stated students, sales, prices, or results.
A course based on US lender platforms and business structures may not fit UK learners without adaptation.
Lou says new inspectors could compete for his own local jobs.

tactics.name: Enter through an experienced inspector and learn on real jobs
steps: Find an experienced draw inspector willing to mentor you.
Go to several inspections with the mentor and learn what the lender's checklist asks you to document.
Use a basic understanding of construction phases and the checklist; Lou says the work is learnable without having personally built a house.
Build skill by documenting the location, progress, and missing items accurately.

quote.text: The easiest way is to get an inspector to kind of mentor you and kind of help you along.
quote.speaker: Lou

tactics.name: Join inspection platforms and price competitively
steps: Sign up with inspection companies and marketplaces that route lender requests.
Review the offered location and fee before accepting a job.
Set a competitive rate when the platform lets you choose; Lou says a high price can send the work to a cheaper inspector.
Build a record of timeliness and thorough reports so lenders and inspection companies continue to use you.

quote.text: I priced myself I think competitively 'cause you kind of set your price. How much you'll do it for.
quote.speaker: Lou

tactics.name: Respond quickly and keep the day flexible
steps: Accept or decline new platform requests promptly.
Call the builder or homeowner to arrange access and give a near-term visit window.
Avoid pinning the whole day to fixed appointment times because new jobs may arrive.
Submit the report within the inspection company's requested 24–48-hour window.

quote.text: I try not to pin myself to a time because my days will change in the drop of a hat.
quote.speaker: Lou

tactics.name: Plan routes and group nearby jobs
steps: The night before, enter the next day's addresses in Google Maps.
Order stops to reduce backtracking and driving time.
When additional jobs arrive in the same area, add them to the route if feasible.
Recheck travel distance and the offered fee before taking a distant job.

quote.text: I'll sit down usually night before and I'll map out the next day's work. I'll get out of Google Maps, I'll plug in where I'm going and I'll look at 'em and then I'll strategically put them in order.
quote.speaker: Lou

tactics.name: Make the inspection evidence easy for the lender to verify
steps: Use parcel data to confirm the property when house numbers or job boxes are missing.
Take a screenshot of the parcel and use it as the first photo in the submission.
Keep phone location settings enabled so photos include location data.
Tell the story of progress with useful photos, including items that are not installed yet.
Use a drone when terrain makes ground-level exterior photos difficult.

quote.text: I take pictures of things that are there and this is gonna sound crazy but I take pictures of the things that are not there.
quote.speaker: Lou

tactics.name: Complete and upload reports on site when connectivity allows
steps: Use the platform app or website required by the company that ordered the inspection.
Upload photos and complete the draw sheet after the visit.
Lou added Starlink to submit from the field where cell signal is weak, avoiding an hour of evening paperwork at home.

quote.text: Buying the Starlink was probably one of the best things I've done. That allowed me to do the inspection on site and submit it.
quote.speaker: Lou

tactics.name: Find short-term rental clients through local relationships
steps: Post in relevant local Facebook pages asking whether owners need property checks.
Contact a local real-estate project manager who manages short-term rentals.
Offer a recurring condition report to owners who live far away.
Price large properties based on the actual time and checklist scope; Lou says he underpriced his first large house.

quote.text: I also reached out to a local project manager with a real estate company and said, "You know, she managed all their short-term rentals."
quote.speaker: Lou

tactics.name: Keep draw inspections within the lender's scope
steps: Report what is installed and what is not installed; do not give credit for materials merely waiting on site.
Avoid taking sides in disputes between homeowners and builders.
Do not present a draw inspection as a judgment on workmanship when the task is to document progress for the lender.

quote.text: We can only give credit for things that are actually installed. So it's gotta be screwed in, set in, set in place.
quote.speaker: Lou

tools_mentioned.purpose: Lou recommends finding an accountant for self-employment and business setup.

warnings.warning: Construction sites can be hazardous. Lou warns about fresh concrete, newly finished floors, elevated decks without handrails, and getting locked behind a door without an exterior handle.

quote.text: Be safe on those construction sites. Make sure you got a point of address and ingress.
quote.speaker: Host

warnings.warning: Do not walk on fresh or protected finishes if doing so could damage them; Lou says he stayed off a floor with a sign warning people not to walk on it.

quote.text: I'm not walking on the floor. I'm Monday's Unate. I'm gonna stay in here and take pictures and get the best I can.
quote.speaker: Lou

warnings.warning: Stay within the lender's task. Lou avoids adjudicating builder disputes or commenting on workmanship beyond documenting whether checklist items are installed.

quote.text: I don't get into any, you know, if they don't like what's going on or they're not happy with this or that, I stay out of that.
quote.speaker: Lou

warnings.warning: Do not give credit for items that are merely on site; Lou says they must actually be installed.

quote.text: We can only give credit for things that are actually installed. So it's gotta be screwed in, set in, set in place.
quote.speaker: Lou

warnings.warning: Short-term rental checks can expose the inspector to liability from guest belongings left in drawers or under beds, including firearms.

quote.text: And it could be anything, firearms to underwear. I mean, it's just all over the map.
quote.speaker: Lou

warnings.warning: Lou says he underpriced his first short-term rental maintenance job, a large seven-bedroom house that took more work than he expected.

quote.text: And it was the initial one I did and I underpriced myself. It was taking me, this was a seven bedroom house on the lake.
quote.speaker: Lou

warnings.warning: Construction activity and geography constrain demand; the work may not suit an area with little construction, and Lou says driving is a major expense.

quote.text: It's probably not for the person that lives in the middle of a desert and there's no construction going on.
quote.speaker: Lou

warnings.warning: Lou says he should consider errors and omissions insurance in addition to his liability policy.

quote.text: I probably should look at an Arizona mission just in case I mess something up, but I really think that the liability covers me pretty well.
quote.speaker: Lou

warnings.warning: Electronic outreach to individuals and sole traders in the UK is restricted by PECR; the Facebook group tactic described should not be extended into unsolicited messages without consent.
Lou says mentoring new local inspectors could create competition for his own work.

quote.text: I don't wanna create the competition that's gonna kill me, but I also don't mind helping people, that would get them in that business and help them along to make some money as well.
quote.speaker: Lou

lessons.lesson: A narrow service can work without deep prior trade experience when the client supplies a checklist and an experienced operator can teach the process.

quote.text: It's not terribly hard. You could probably YouTube how a house is built, and there's probably a video out there and exactly what the phases are and figure it out pretty easily.
quote.speaker: Lou

lessons.lesson: A mentor can shorten the path to a first job by showing a newcomer what to observe and how to report it.

quote.text: The easiest way is to get an inspector to kind of mentor you and kind of help you along.
quote.speaker: Lou

lessons.lesson: For local field work, route planning and geographic density matter because driving can take more time than the task itself.

quote.text: I spend more time behind a windshield than I do on the job site.
quote.speaker: Lou

lessons.lesson: Build reliability through prompt, thorough work; repeat platform and lender work depends on being timely and dependable.

quote.text: I appreciate your timeliness and you're always there and you say what you're gonna say and you're thorough.
quote.speaker: Lou

lessons.lesson: Document absences as well as completed work when the customer needs an accurate view of progress.

quote.text: I take pictures of things that are there and this is gonna sound crazy but I take pictures of the things that are not there.
quote.speaker: Lou

lessons.lesson: Price a service around its full scope and time, especially when a property or job is larger than expected.

quote.text: And it was the initial one I did and I underpriced myself.
quote.speaker: Lou

lessons.lesson: Stay in the role the customer hired you for and avoid taking responsibility for disputes or judgments outside that scope.

quote.text: I don't get into any, you know, if they don't like what's going on or they're not happy with this or that, I stay out of that.
quote.speaker: Lou

lessons.lesson: Keep side-hustle capacity aligned with the life you want; Lou chose not to push for full-time growth after becoming busy.

quote.text: I didn't want to make it. I don't want to be full time again.
quote.speaker: Lou

lessons.lesson: Act on a promising idea while motivation is present instead of waiting indefinitely.

quote.text: So take that, take action, do something with it.
quote.speaker: Lou

lessons.lesson: A repeatable service can create room for adjacent income streams, such as adding property checks or teaching the process to others.

quote.text: I've also granched out and I jumped into something with short-term rentals and tried to make that work.
quote.speaker: Lou

evidence_quality.rationale: Lou describes his own work process, acquisition routes, equipment, schedule, and operating costs in useful detail. Several financial figures are specific but not independently verified, and parts of the Whisper transcript appear to garble words and numbers, including his initial monthly income target and some platform names. Commercial inspections and the planned training business are not established results.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: The host reads paid advertisements for Gusto, Wealthfront, Shopify, and Quo; the Wealthfront read explicitly says it is a paid non-client endorsement. Lou is also preparing a draw inspector training website and course, but gives no price or sales results.
